title: He is the ATP player who became world number one despite losing six first round matches in a row
description: There have been 29 different men who have held the number one singles ranking on the ATP Tour. Jannik Sinner is the 29th of those...
fullText:
There have been 29 different men who have held the number one singles ranking on the ATP Tour.

Jannik Sinner is the 29th of those world number ones, with his current ongoing reign lasting 24 weeks, having topped the ATP rankings for a total of 90 weeks across his three spells.

Despite this, Sinner is under threat of losing his number one to Alexander Zverev, who has won two Grand Slams this year and is currently on track to end the year as the top-ranked player in men's tennis.

Zverev is now in a similar position to what Yevgeny Kafelnikov was in back in 1999, but he will be hoping that if he does become world number one, it happens in a more successful fashion than it did for the Russian 27 years ago.

Kafelnikov came into the 1999 season as the world number 11, but had previously been ranked as high as world number three.

The Russian very quickly returned to the top 10, as Kafelnikov won the Australian Open, his second Grand Slam title after Roland Garros in 1996.

This propelled Kafelnikov back up to his previous career-high of world number three, as he closed in on the world number one ranking, which was then held by Pete Sampras, who did not play the Australian Open due to physical and mental fatigue.

Kafelnikov continued this form into the indoor season, where he won the title at the Rotterdam Open after beating a young Roger Federer, as well as British players Greg Rusedski and then Tim Henman in the final.

This placed Kafelnikov as the world number two heading into the sunshine double of Indian Wells and the Miami Open, but neither tournament went to plan for him.

Kafelnikov lost his only match at both Indian Wells and the Miami Open, and after winning two matches in the Davis Cup, he was hoping to rediscover his form upon his return to the ATP Tour for the clay court season.

This did not happen for Kafelnikov, who lost in the first round of all four of his next clay-court tournaments. Three of these four players Kafelnikov would lose to were ranked outside the top 60, including then world number 196 Ivan Ljubicic beating him in Monte Carlo.

Despite Kafelnikov losing in the first round of six tournaments in a row, he became world number one after being beaten by world number 72 Richard Fromberg and overtook Sampras, who dropped 144 points after being absent due to a back injury, at the top of the ATP rankings.

Yevygeny Kafelnikov's losing streak before becoming No.1

Gustavo Kuerten beat Kafelnikov, 0-6 7-6(4) 6-3

Vincent Spadea beat Kafelnikov, 6(6)-7 7-6(4) 6-2

Andrei Pavel beat Kafelnikov, 6-3 2-6 6-3

Franco Squillari beat Kafelnikov, 6-2 6-4

Ivan Ljubicic beat Kafelnikov, 6-1 6-2

Richard Fromberg beat Kafelnikov, 6-4 2-6 6-4

Kafelnikov ended his run of six successive first-round losses at his next tournament in Rome, but his relatively poor form still continued after becoming world number one.

In his four tournaments as world number one, Kafelnikov won just six of his 10 matches, which culminated after losing in the first round of the Queen's Club Championships.

Sampras won the title at Queen's, and therefore dethroned world number one Kafelnikov, who dropped down to world number three after also falling below Pat Rafter.

Tournaments Kafelnikov played as world number one

Third Round – Lost to Gustavo Kuerten (No.14)

Hypo Group Tennis International (St.Poelten)

Semi-final – Lost to Mariano Zabaleta (No.26)

Second Round – Lost to Dominik Hrbaty (No.30)

First Round – Lost to Sargis Sargsian (No.74)

Kafelnikov's one and only run as world number one lasted a total of six weeks, which is one of the lowest in ATP history, equal to Marcelo Rios and Thomas Muster.

Only Carlos Moya (2) and Rafter (1) have had short reigns as world number one, with both also taking place during the 1999 season.

title: US edge opening session of Presidents Cup
description: The US begin their bid to win an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup by opening up a 3-2 lead over the International team on day one.
fullText:
The United States began their bid to win an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup by opening up a 3-2 lead over the International team at the end of Thursday's fourballs matches at Medinah Country Club in Illinois.

Justin Thomas and rookie Jackson Koivun put the first point on the board for Brandt Snedeker's American team with a resounding 4&3 win over Canada's Corey Conners and Colombia's Nico Echavarria.

World number one Scottie Scheffler, who was partnered with his long-time friend Sam Burns, took the 17th hole and held on to close out their victory over Min Woo Lee and Sungjae Im, who were left to rue several missed putts down the stretch.

And two-time major champions Wyndham Clark and Collin Morikawa ensured the US would take an advantage into Friday's five foursome matches.

Clark and Morikawa led from the opening hole against Australia's Adam Scott and reigning Open champion Ryan Fox before completing their 3&2 success with two holes to spare.

"A session win is a session win; we're going to take it any way we can get it," said Snedeker.

However, Geoff Ogilvy's International side will head into the alternate shot format on Friday with optimism of remaining in contention to claim only their second ever triumph in the biennial contest, some 28 years after their first in 1998.

Japanese duo Hideki Matsuyama and debutant Ryo Hisatsune recorded a 3&1 success over Cameron Young and Xander Schauffele, while Kim Si-woo and Tom Kim always looked comfortable in their 3&2 win over Chris Gotterup and Patrick Cantlay.

The five foursome matches scheduled to take place on Friday will be followed by two sessions on Saturday, split between four four-ball matches in the morning and four foursomes in the afternoon.

All 12 players on each team will then compete in the singles matches on Sunday, with 15½ points required for overall victory.

title: Maeda makes Premier League intensity claim after Celtic move
description: Daizen Maeda has admitted he is still adapting to the demands of English football following his summer departure from Celtic.The Japanese international swapped Glasgow for Ipswich Town after a hugely ...
fullText:
Daizen Maeda has admitted he is still adapting to the demands of English football following his summer departure from Celtic.

The Japanese international swapped Glasgow for Ipswich Town after a hugely productive spell at Parkhead, where his pace, relentless pressing and movement made him one of Celtic's most distinctive attacking players.

Those qualities are now being tested in a considerably different environment.

Speaking to Japanese media, Maeda admitted: "I'm playing at an intensity I've never experienced before. First of all, it's important to get used to it."

The forward also acknowledged that the attributes which proved so effective in Scotland have required adjustment.

"In Scotland my strengths were speed and high pressing, but the intensity is completely different," he said.

Maeda's departure removed a player who had been instrumental to Celtic's pressing structure and attacking threat. Celtic's title success of last year coincided with Daizen finding his shooting boots culminating in the late winner against Hearts.

The move to England was richly deserved for a player that gave Celtic so much. Hopefully he can kick on and make a real fist of it.

His early experiences in England underline the scale of that transition, although the 28-year-old remains enthusiastic about testing himself against leading opposition.

For Celtic, meanwhile, replacing the Japanese forward's combination of goals, pace and defensive work remains a significant challenge.

title: Felix gives Portugal win over Wales as Ronaldo misfires
description: Joao Felix scored the only goal with a long-range shot as reigning Nations League champions Portugal opened their campaign with a 1-0 home win over Wales. Every time the 41-year-old, who made his national debut in 2003 and has since scored a record 146 international goals, touched the ball near the goal, the roar of the home crowd rose several octaves.
fullText:
Joao Felix scored the only goal with a long-range shot as reigning Nations League champions Portugal opened their campaign with a 1-0 home win over Wales.

Portugal, who have won two of the four finals since the competition was launched in 2018, dominated possession and outshot Wales 19-4 in Lisbon but squandered a string of chances.

Their only goal came after 22 minutes when a low scuffed shot by Felix from the edge of the box took a slight deflection off Wales captain Ben Davies and skipped inside the far post beyond Danny Ward's desperate dive.

As it has for some two decades, Portugal's attack revolved around Cristiano Ronaldo. Every time the 41-year-old, who made his national debut in 2003 and has since scored a record 146 international goals, touched the ball near the goal, the roar of the home crowd rose several octaves.

Ronaldo found the side netting once and shinned an inviting volley high over from close range. After an hour he slid the ball into the Wales net but, to his evident disbelief, was ruled offside.

He was still shaking his head when he was replaced seven minutes later.

The crowd grew quieter and Portugal's play drifted after Ronaldo's departure.

Wales came agonisingly close to equalising, twice, from their one good chance.

First, Brennan Johnson chipped goalkeeper Diogo Costa and hit the face of the bar. With Costa stranded, Lewis Koumas and Dan James both went for the rebound. Koumas ended up shooting tamely straight at defender Ruben Dias on the line.

fullText:
Sept 24 (Reuters) - US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.

The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the ‌global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.

The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's ‌stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.

A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.

"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would ​be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.

Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."

A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States."

Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that ‌was "collapsing."

The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran's economy and left ⁠Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.

Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.

"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," Ross said.

A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ⁠ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.

Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.

After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.

The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.

Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.

This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than ​for ​preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the ​risk of escalation grows.

Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with ‌Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.

"Our fingers are on the trigger," said the senior Iranian official. "The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low."

Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.

Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran's position, the regional sources said.

The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.

This month, it targeted Iran's remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards. Trump warned that Iran's economy could "rot" unless it reached a deal.

"Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway," he ‌said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait."

At the heart of the diplomacy in New ​York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways ​to become enduring bargaining chips.

FEARS OF AN OPEN-ENDED CONFLICT

During a separate meeting with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington's ​endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.

They conveyed their collective rejection of any Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of navigation must be restored and that the strategic ‌waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.

Yet alongside their warnings over ​Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the ​region's determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.

"It's still not clear what Trump's endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center think tank based in Abu Dhabi.

"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to define its roadmap," she said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

That ​uncertainty is also shaping Tehran's calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer, said the ‌New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.

"The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their ​position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften their position, they are dead," said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.

A Western official familiar with the talks added: "It is all about opening the Strait ​of Hormuz. We're all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that."

(Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington; Writing by Samia Nakhoul, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

title: Kinsella makes GB return for Worlds a year after giving birth
description: Olympic bronze medallist Alice Kinsella is named in the Great Britain team for the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships just a year after giving birth.
fullText:
Olympic bronze medallist Alice Kinsella says it is "completely surreal" to have been named in the Great Britain team for the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships just a year after giving birth.

She has been selected to compete in Rotterdam between 17-25 October alongside world medallists Abigail Martin, Ruby Evans, Becky Downie and Alia Leat.

The 25-year-old, a two-time European champion, became the first British artistic gymnast to resume competition after giving birth when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.

"I can't put into words with how I'm feeling right now, my goal was always to be ready to compete properly next year and to now say I'm going to the World Championships just feels completely surreal," said Kinsella, who also got married over the summer.

"I feel so incredibly proud of this achievement. To think I'm going to the World Championships just over a year postpartum is insane.

"It's been a tough year but I don't regret my decision in coming back to elite sport at all, it was always the goal of mine and there was nothing stopping me from reaching that goal.

"I can't wait to tell this story to Parker when he's all grown up, it's a big one to tell!"

Double world champion Jake Jarman will participate in the men's event in the Netherlands along with Olympic bronze medallist Harry Hepworth.

Scotland's Reuben Ward, three-time world medal winner Joe Fraser and double world medallist Courtney Tulloch will also feature for Britain.

title: 'The lads wanted me to stick one up him' - Wood relives fastest spells
description: As England bowler Mark Wood retires from international cricket, he talks through his most famous spells from his Test career.
fullText:
When Mark Wood retired on Tuesday, he brought to an end one of the most entertaining England careers in recent years.

The fastest England bowler on record by most metrics, he produced a number of thrilling spells in a career too often hit by injuries.

Here are four of those spells in his own words...

Despite bowling quickly on occasions, Wood averaged 41.73 with the ball across his first 12 Tests. Then, on the advice of West Indies legend Michael Holding, he lengthened his run-up and using it for the first time, took 5-41 in the first innings of the third Test against West Indies in Saint Lucia in 2019.

"That was the fastest. I could be biased because I thought it was a breakthrough moment in my career but when I was watching the ball carry off the nicks, they felt a long way in the slips.

"You feel weightless, like you're never tired and are just picking up speed. It feels like you have all of this momentum and loose energy to release. You feel a surge through your body and then a whip out of your fingers.

"That day I didn't have to try. Root could have put the field anywhere and I wouldn't have cared. I was so up in my action. I can remember my feet landing and the feeling of the balls on my fingers - the seam ripping up my fingers.

"I essentially had two different careers – the first one in and out of the team with good moments but struggling with ankle injuries and form. I felt I had to constantly push myself with that stop-start run-up to get the most out of myself.

"As soon as I went off my longer run I had much more momentum, flow and freedom and the ability to bowl consistently quicker for longer.

"When I lengthened my run-up, if it was below 90mph I was annoyed."

Wood's best match figures are 9-100 from the fourth Test against South Africa in Johannesburg in 2020. On a quick and bouncy pitch, Wood averaged 89.1mph and helped England secure a 191-win run.

"I faced [South Africa bowler] Anrich Nortje there and when he bowled a bouncer I could hear it go past me. I was honestly so scared but something clicked in me that I would bowl fast.

"I got Rassie van der Dussen for 98 caught from round the wicket. We double-bluffed him. That was a great wicket because he was giving us a bit of verbals back.

"Faf du Plessis wasn't happy with something and Van der Dussen got involved.

"The way he commands a presence at the crease winds people up and he has a little bit of verbals here and there.

"A few of the lads were desperate for me to stick one up him.

"We set up this bouncer plan, I pitched it up and he hit it straight to cover."

Wood's best innings figures came at the end of the 2021-22 Ashes defeat when he took 6-37 in the second innings of the final Test in Hobart.

"It is disappointing because you are losing but you still have the pride in your own performance. You have to have pride in your performance.

"I wanted to do it for Spoons [coach Chris Silverwood]. He was under a lot of pressure but was really good for me and backed me up - Jon Lewis the bowling coach as well.

"I played four out of the five Tests and was proud of that. I was so tired at the end of that spell but came out with my best figures of the tour.

"[The Australian public] respected that I kept trying and bowling quickly. Even on the boundary line the Australia fans were saying 'Woody, we want to see you on'.

"[Afterwards] I was in the lift with Justin Langer and he put his hand up and pulled me in and said 'respect'.

"That was a really nice moment. We always want respect from our people but to have it from the Australians was nice."

Wood will likely be best remembered for his devastating 5-34 in the first innings of the third Ashes Test at Headingley in 2023. With Australia 2-0 up in the series, Wood averaged 90.4mph on day one and transformed the series in an electric spell of pace bowling, famously dismissing Australia opener Usman Khawaja.

"I was absolutely ready to go. The day before I was bowling to a mitt and the strength coach had to swap because it was hurting his hand so much.

"I can still hear the commentary and feel the ball.

"It was a special moment because my parents were here as well. It was the first time they saw me get five wickets.

"I spent a lot of my career in the bouncer role. I thought at times I was better than that and it hurt my stats.

"That day I got to pitch it up and it was the swing that did it.

"The BBC had [the Khawaja wicket] on socials and I watched it so many times. I just loved the noise it made. I wish I could bottle that up."

title: Buttler injury halts England as Sri Lanka level series
description: Jos Buttler's bravery comes in vain as Sri Lanka fight back to beat England in the second one-day international at Headingley and set up a series decider at The Oval.
fullText:
Second Metro Bank one-day international, Headingley

Sri Lanka 321-6 (50 overs): Kusal 121, Kamindu 54; Ahmed 2-48

England 305-9 (50 overs): Banton 73, Buttler 69; Wellalage 3-49

Jos Buttler's bravery came in vain as Sri Lanka fought back to beat England in the second one-day international at Headingley and set up a series decider at The Oval.

Needing 68 from 75 balls, England were cruising towards a target of 322 until Buttler retired hurt on 67 after tweaking a hamstring.

When Rehan Ahmed, Gus Atkinson and Jamie Overton fell, Buttler re-emerged with 27 needed from 14 balls and witnessed Will Jacks fall for 52 at the non-striker's end.

England were left needing 19 from the last with Buttler on strike but, barely able to hobble a single, he holed out at deep mid-wicket. England finished on 306-9 as Sri Lanka won by 16 runs.

Buttler had earlier shown flashes of his vintage best in hitting Sri Lanka's spinners for five sixes, putting England on course after collapse of 3-14 spoiled an opening stand of 143 between Tom Banton and Ben Duckett.

Sri Lanka were fortunate for the way he was abruptly halted but deserve credit for the way their seamers used reverse swing afterwards to deny England's lower order.

Their captain Kusal Mendis also hit a fine 122 in their 321-6. The series, and the international summer, concludes on Sunday from 10:30 BST.

'The lads wanted me to stick one up him' - Wood relives fastest spells

Sri Lanka level ODI series as England fall short in thriller - as it happened

Pick your County Championship team of the season

What to make of this dramatic encounter? It is a defeat for England, one which halts their momentum a touch as they build towards next year's 50-over World Cup.

It was unlike any other, however. They will do well to find situations like these again when the bigger moments come.

"It is always disappointing when you lose," captain Harry Brook said.

"Sri Lanka played exceptionally well there, especially the last 10-15 overs. There were plenty of moments in the game we could have been slightly better."

One positive was the batting of Buttler before injury struck. He has not scored a century in this format for three-and-a-half years and had his T20 form doubted earlier this year at the World Cup.

The way he took down the spinners was brutal. When he was flying, England were on course for their highest chase at this ground.

The opening stand between Banton and Duckett was also impressive - reminiscent of England's brightest ODIs days as they thrashed around the bowling at more than seven runs an over.

That neither pressed on - Duckett was bowled for 67 and Banton stumped for 73, both to left-arm spinner Dinuth Wellalage - was disappointing. There were also rare failures for Joe Root who made 15 and Brook, the latter also pinned in front lbw for one by Wellalage.

Perhaps more concerning was that the lower order were unable to support Jacks in his quest to push England over the line again.

That aspect must improve over England's three white-ball series that come before mid-January.

This has been a difficult tour for Sri Lanka, who were outclassed in the 3-0 T20 series defeat and well beaten by 89 runs in the first ODI at Chester-le-Street.

This, especially given the bad start with the ball, will be a significant boost to morale.

Kusal was troubled early on by Overton's bouncers, top-edging one into a gap soon after Atkinson dropped a simple chance at fine leg when the right-hander had 17 - another England error. The Sri Lanka captain also had to overturn a caught-behind decision on 99 when Overton was the bowler again.

Kusal was eventually caught on the boundary trying to clear deep mid-wicket off Ahmed, who also had Charith Asalanka caught in the same position for 2-48 but did not offer the control usually brought by Adil Rashid.

A flat Headingley pitch was a far bigger test of England's seamers than Tuesday's difficult surface in Durham.

Josh Tongue struggled with his lines for 0-50 in seven overs. Atkinson, who took 2-55, and Overton, who had another catch dropped in the final over, in taking 0-63 from 10 were England's best bowling performers.

"Tight games are always good games to watch and good games to be a part of," Brook added.

"Having the opportunity to play in a decider will only benefit us."

title: Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?

Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!

This particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has a dedicated page aggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.

Consumers have noticed. Reportedly an estimated 39% of Americans canceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Another survey indicates that a majority of people Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.

To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.

The reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?

Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.

That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-based Tubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.

Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you, Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcom where they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.

Still, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.

There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.

title: Global bond sell-off piles new pressure on UK borrowing costs before budget
description: Rising cost of 10-year gilt to near 19-year high hikes upfront cost of government investment and limits chancellor’s room for...
fullText:
Rising cost of 10-year gilt to near 19-year high hikes upfront cost of government investment and limits chancellor’s room for manoeuvre

International bodies warn of rising debt and borrowing risks

Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

A global sell-off in government bonds has put fresh upward pressure on UK borrowing costs, before a tough budget for John Healey next month.

The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, had risen to 5.38% by mid-morning on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.

Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.

Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that the former chancellor Rachel Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.

Healey, her successor, has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn.

Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts; but Treasury sources insist the budget will be “focused”, with important spending decisions postponed to a review next year.

Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling prompted by fears of higher inflation and interest rates as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on.

The Bank of England chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that UK interest rates would have to rise.

“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland.

“On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”

Higher rates would mean increased mortgage costs for homeowners, at a time when Andy Burnham’s government has promised to offer consumers a “breathing space” against the rising cost of living.

The Bank is also expecting an eye-watering 24% rise in the quarterly energy price cap that determines household utility bills in January, if oil prices remain high.

Lombardelli’s message echoed that of the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, after the nine-member monetary policy committee left interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week.

She stressed that high oil prices had had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank had feared; but the longer they remained high, the greater the risk of inflation becoming entrenched.

As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 30-year US Treasury bonds surged to 5.444% – the highest level since 2004.

Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

description: USA international Emily Fox has described signed a new contract at Arsenal as "an easy decision".
fullText:
USA international Emily Fox has described her decision to sign a new contract at Arsenal as "an easy decision".

The 28-year-old has been a key player for the club since joining from North Carolina Courage in 2024 and is understood to have signed a new three-year deal.

She was part of the squad that won the Women's Champions League title in 2025 and the Women's Champions Cup trophy in 2026.

In her first season at the club, she won the Women's League Cup and has been named in the PFA team of the year in the last two campaigns.

Speaking to BBC Sport, she said: "I'm very pleased to be able to continue my journey with Arsenal and it was honestly an easy decision because of where I want to be now, and in a few years' time.

"When I think of how I'm going to grow, be challenged and be in an environment where it's like my second home, I think of Arsenal.

"It is a club that is wanting to continue to push the women's game, invest in it and focus on the community, the history of it, the culture, and wanting to excel."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

BBC Sport reported in January that Fox had a year remaining on her existing contract but Arsenal were always confident she would stay at the club.

She has established herself as one of the best full-backs in the world and has made almost 100 appearances for Arsenal in all competitions.

However, despite helping Renee Slegers' side to European glory in 2025, Fox feels there is one important medal missing from her collection - the WSL title.

"There is definitely some unfinished business. We want to keep going, keep winning and maybe get some things that we've already won before too," said Fox.

"Being at Arsenal, there's always going to be high expectations from the inside and the outside. That's just part of it.

"When you have big goals like that, you have to take it game-by-game and you can't look too far ahead. That's my approach."

Fox is also preparing for a big summer with the USA, under the management of ex-Chelsea boss Emma Hayes, as they hope to go far at the 2027 Women's World Cup.

"We're starting off strong by playing Spain twice at home in October. This year has been great for us in terms of the opponents and the challenges," she added.

"I feel like we've played a lot of variety with our opponents and it's given us a taste of different environments, different tactics and layers of how we're going to play.

"That's ultimately what you need to do when you want to win a World Cup. In November, we have to qualify. Those are our objectives."

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington is getting a much chillier reception on Capitol Hill than at the White House as lawmakers from both parties use the visit to denounce China's actions on the world stage.

Lawmakers have long found little downside to taking a hawkish tone on China, but the U.S.'s war with Iran has inflamed tensions as U.S. officials accuse China of propping up Iran's economy and supplying its military with components and intelligence, endangering U.S. service members in the Middle East.

In speeches, letters, press conferences and hearings, lawmakers from both parties aired criticism of Xi's visit. Their actions and events stand in stark contrast to the warm welcome that Trump gave Xi on Wednesday as he arrived in Washington for a lavish state visit.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, took to the Senate floor Tuesday night, offering a list of issues for Trump to raise with Xi, but not before suggesting that Xi shouldn't have been asked to visit Washington at all.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said.

Wicker seemed particularly taken aback by the honor of a state dinner. Over the salad course, Wicker said the president could ask Xi about the Chinese Navy's harassment of Filipino fishermen and sailors. Then, while the servers are "switching from chardonnay to cabernet at the fancy state dinner," perhaps the president could turn to the issue of Taiwan, he said.

He went on to say he hopes some progress will be made when the president discussed trade and artificial intelligence with Xi. But concluded with this: "During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."

Ahead of Xi's visit, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a highly critical video that had been viewed more than 245,000 times on X. In the video, the committee details Xi's rise to power starting in 1974 and ends by labeling him "the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world."

The House created the panel in 2023. It's held several hearings on human rights issues in China and advocates for legislation on an array of economic and military issues. For example, the committee's chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., recently introduced a bill that would prohibit the manufacture or sale of Chinese cars in the U.S.

Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and three other Republican senators used the Xi visit to press the Trump administration to move ahead with aid and arms sales to Taiwan.

In a letter, they reminded Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he had previously stated that "deterring an invasion of Taiwan must be our top priority." And they noted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had once declared that the U.S. "will not let our allies and partners be subordinated and intimidated."

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

"It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific," the senators wrote, "if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and three other Democratic senators held a press conference to warn against the U.S. weakening export controls for advanced semiconductor chips and equipment. They're concerned that such exports could erase the U.S.'s lead in artificial intelligence over China.

They touched on voter concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence and contrasted Democrats' call for greater regulation with the president's call to "encourage it, not rein it in."

"We must reject the false choice Trump keeps making," Schumer told reporters. "We can and must both maintain our lead on AI by restricting China's access to our technology and put up guardrails to mitigate AI's risk."

Meanwhile, on the Senate floor, Democratic senators urged Trump to confront Xi directly about the support his country is providing Iran.

"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.

fullText:
They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships

Professors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world of Pokémon (apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.

But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.

I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.

The official Pokémon website describes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.

Gemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.

“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”

Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)

Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.

For her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.

“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”

De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed. However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.

“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”

A difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at the Pokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself in a statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.

I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?

“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”

Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by the Pokémon Company.

title: Mamdani and Spain's PM build ties as the left looks to counter the far right
description:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S.
fullText:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.

Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S. politicians and kindred figures abroad as they seek to forge ties to counter the rise of right-wing populism.

Organizers behind these formal and informal gatherings say the efforts to bring together U.S. left-leaning Democrats in office and their ideological counterparts aim to contend with the well-organized, growing international movement of populists in step with President Donald Trump's administration, as the anti-immigrant and nationalist Alternative for Germany party gains traction, and France's Marine Le Pen and her party, National Rally, lead in polls ahead of a presidential race next year.

Wednesday's event at Gracie Mansion, Mamdani's residence, was billed as focused on "building an economy for the many." Sánchez touted the success of Spain's minimum-wage increases as "proving that another economic model is possible."

"That is why the powerful fear us. Because day after day, we show that a different path is possible, and it works," Sánchez said at the event, which also included the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, and European Council President António Costa, who is a former socialist prime minister of Portugal.

Mamdani nodded to the efforts to collaborate with like-minded leaders, telling attendees, "It is truly a privilege to be able to learn from one another, emulate each others successes and develop strategies that imitate the great progress those in this room have achieved."

Heading into the U.N. General Assembly, Mamdani over the weekend hosted left-leaning mayors from Paris, Barcelona, Rome, Amsterdam, Mexico City and elsewhere for a summit on housing, migration and climate change. And he met this week with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, a social democrat in the same general tradition as Sánchez.

In April, politicians and world leaders convened in Barcelona for the first Global Progressive Mobilization conference, which was touted by organizers as an "alternative to conservative and far-right forces."

The event included prerecorded remarks from democratic socialists Mamdani and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who revitalized that tradition in U.S. politics. But it also opened up the tent to include speeches from Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz - the 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee who served as a moderate "Blue Dog" Democrat in Congress - and Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who has embraced economic populism and urged his party to connect with voters it lost in 2024.

Giacomo Filibeck, who served on the organizing committee for April's conference, told The Washington Post that the participation of the U.S. Democrats was "instrumental" in showing how the global progressive movement can work together.

"In a nutshell, we have been rediscovering our internationalism that maybe in the past years was a bit put on the side," he added.

Democrats have long sought friends abroad. As U.S. president, especially in his first term, Barack Obama courted widespread international goodwill. But he forged a special bond with Angela Merkel of Germany's Christian Democratic Union, a center-right party at least in European terms - a different segment of the Western political spectrum than the one Mamdani is courting.

Socialists and other left-wing activists also have long organized internationally. The Sanders presidential campaign built ties to equivalent movements in Europe. The New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, from which Mamdani emerged, last year hosted Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the perennial French presidential candidate and founder of the hard-left party La France Insoumise.

But as energy coalesces in the left wing of the Democratic Party - with the electoral success of some candidates aligned with or backed by the DSA, Mamdani most prominent among them - the global bridge-building has taken on a new urgency.

Johan Hassel, a senior fellow and director of Global Progress Action (GPA) at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank in Washington, said Trump's reelection in 2024 was "a game changer" that helped unify global progressives.

GPA has arranged high-level meetings between U.S. officials and center-left leaders abroad. Its most recent public convening, in Toronto this past May, included appearances by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), former U.S. transportation secretary and potential 2028 candidate Pete Buttigieg, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The left traditionally has seen more of their differences … than their similarities. I think this is changing," Hassel said. "You're starting to see a larger democratic bloc of center-left liberals, Greens. The left that understands that something … larger is at stake."

Such politicians and movements within the U.S. and abroad, he said, "are inspiring each other" as a result of their alliances. Among the examples, he cited Mamdani's embrace of social investment in child care and housing, akin to policies long adopted by European social democrats.

Conversely, European left-wing party members made the pilgrimage to New York to canvass for Mamdani in the final weeks of his campaign. Members of Germany's anti-capitalist party Die Linke (the Left) traveled to New York to learn more about Mamdani's effort and met with his advisers.

Die Linke, whose platform is focused on lowering the cost of living and using state interventions to address the German capital's housing shortage, went on to secure a historic win in the Berlin state election Sunday.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people.

"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic.

"We could lose control of the future to AI," said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn't concentrated in one company or country.

For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?

The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late?

The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that's not hyperbole but something that's already a reality or at least perilously close.

title: GB sniff Road Worlds chance with Pogacar absent
description: British riders stand a strong chance of glory at cycling's Road World Championships this weekend, with young talent beginning to blossom at elite level.
fullText:
Great Britain's impressive rider line-up for cycling's Road World Championships means the team have rarely stood a better chance of glory.

For the men, there is also the helpful factor of Slovenian superstar Tadej Pogacar being absent, after he suffered crash injuries during the Vuelta a Espana in August.

But at the same time a new generation of British cycling talent is rising, and GB riders could take the coveted winner's rainbow jersey in the men's and women's road races in Montreal this weekend.

While Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta, the race showcased the continued emergence of 21-year-old British rider Matthew Brennan, who won five stages of the three-week endurance test for Visma Lease a Bike - a record for a Grand Tour debutant.

There are currently 49 British riders competing across the men's and women's world tours - more than ever before - and some of those will compete in this World Championship weekend.

The road race itself is much like a stage of the Tour de France, but in which riders compete in national squads, looking to out-think and out-muscle each other.

A lot of the British potential is thanks to the inspiration of British cycling's golden period, which featured great success from the likes of Team Sky, Mark Cavendish and Lizzie Deignan across the past 15 years.

Deignan won the road race in 2015, while Cavendish triumphed in 2011.

In total, British riders have won the elite road races seven times, including Tom Simpson (1965), Beryl Burton (1960 & 1967), Mandy Jones (1982) and Nicole Cooke (2008).

Amid an unpredictable performance landscape for the women, Britain's best young female riders have a chance to infiltrate the once-dominant Dutch contingent.

Tour de France Femmes winner Demi Vollering remains the sport's best overall, but Briton Zoe Backstedt's brilliant second place in Sunday's Worlds time trial was her first shot at the elite level.

She will be involved in Saturday's women's road race, and Olympic mountain bike gold medallist and Tour de France stage winner Tom Pidcock will race for the men on Sunday.

"You need a lot of faith in your team to be present at the front," Backstedt told BBC Sport. "You need to talk, hear, see and feel each other to know they are there, especially as there's no team radio.

"Obviously it's about knowing the big names to follow. If Demi or Kasia [Niewiadoma] go off the front, you know it's a dangerous move and you need to be there.

"But we've got a super strong team, and if any one of us was with them, we all could stand have a chance."

The women's road race is 180.4km long, which includes eight laps of Montreal, and the men's 273.2km race incorporates 12 circuits.

More Then the Score: How cyclists escape to victory

One key way to win a road race at the Road Worlds is by breaking away from the peloton with a certain distance of the race left to run.

The risk is that one, or a handful, of cyclists find it much harder to win a race by riding into the wind than a peloton of more than 100 riders all taking turns in what can be known as the 'washing machine effect'.

But, if the legs are good and the wind is with them, riders can break away for glory.

"Sometimes you are surprised when you hit the wall, but other times you can push harder and dig deeper," Norway's Sigrid Haugset told the BBC's More Than the Score podcast.

The Uno-X Mobility rider won stage three of this year's Tour de France Femmes after a huge 113km breakaway in which she beat more decorated rivals, such as Belgium's Lotte Kopecky.

"That's the good day - when you feel unstoppable. But I like it when there is plenty of noise [on the team radio from the car]. If it's too little, you get into your head, you feel a bit alone."

Steve Cummings is sporting director at World Tour team Jayco Alula and a former GB rider and breakaway stage winner on both the 2015 and 2016 Tours de France.

Assessing the thrill of a breakaway win, he told More Than the Score: "It's like an underdog victory, and it kind of warms the heart. You have to go all-in. It becomes unpredictable and things can happen tactically and physically - say if a rider pushes too much on a climb.

"That day [in 2015] I did the climb of my life. I was empty for two days after [the 2016 win] and I was in bed for two days after [a Dauphine stage win]. It takes a lot out of you."

title: The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winner
description: Martyn Jackson never thought he'd play football again when he had a heart transplant in 2024. Less than two years later, he was a World Cup winner with England.
fullText:
When Martyn Jackson walked off the pitch after Ramsbottom United's 2-1 win over Cheadle Town in October 2024, it never crossed his mind that one day he could be a World Cup winner.

In fact, in the days after that match, his goal was just staying alive.

Just a couple of days after the final whistle, Jackson started to feel unwell during the night.

He went into hospital and was diagnosed with myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart usually caused by an infection. Within weeks, he was placed on the super urgent waiting list for a transplant.

His life was saved when a donor heart became available, and on 28 November 2024, he had successful surgery at Wythenshawe Hospital in Greater Manchester.

Fast forward to September 2026, and Jackson scored for England in their 5-1 win over Spain in the final of the Transplant Football World Cup.

His team-mates and opponents were, like him, all recipients of a donor organ.

"Obviously, when you've had a transplant, you don't think you're ever going to play again. That's what I thought anyway," Jackson tells BBC Sport.

"I'll be forever grateful to my donor and the family for what they've given me. They've given me the gift of life and the opportunity to live my life to the fullest."

Football at the Transplant World Cup is not quite the same as the game played at the Fifa World Cup.

Instead, it reflects how delicate each player's body is having been through life-altering surgery.

Matches are seven-a-side and played over 20-minute halves. Contact is "not as aggressive as I was used to", Jackson says.

Having played 11-a-side football in the ninth tier of English football before his surgery, he became a game-changing new addition to the national transplant team when he joined up with the squad in January 2026.

Jackson spent his youth career in the academy at Manchester United, before spells at Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End and Burnley. He eventually stopped pursuing a career as a professional and spent 13 years with clubs across the non-league pyramid.

During his recovery, wife Lucy heard about the opportunity to join an England Transplant FC team on social media.

Daley Cross, manager of the England team, said of Lucy's role: "She was just trying to do her best for him and trying to find a way to motivate him.

"His wife did drop in the conversation that he used to play at Manchester United as a schoolboy. So that got our ears twitched instantly.

"You could tell from him being on the pitch, even though he was so fresh into his journey, that he knew the football game and he would be such an incredible asset to us.

"You can be in a dark place, at the time of diagnosis, through your treatment or even post-transplant. So to have us exist to help and inspire people means that we are getting some incredible footballers.

"And that really is the power of it: to that transplant community or to the world, showing people that when you've had organ failure, your life isn't over. There is a chance for you, and you can go and resume and live your life."

As the recipient of a donor heart, Jackson has to manage his exercise workload more carefully than his team-mates, many of whom have had kidney transplants, the most common transplant in the UK.

His role in the side tends to involve 10-minute bursts, rather than playing for the duration of matches.

Bayern Munich's Alphonso Davies was diagnosed with a mild form of myocarditis in 2022. He was sidelined for nearly five months, undergoing specialist cardiac monitoring, before returning to play.

Jackson started to feel ill two days after Ramsbottom side's win over Cheadle, and his case became so severe that doctors had to fit his heart with a mechanical pump to keep him alive.

"Of course it was extremely scary," he says, "but at that stage, when you are critically ill, there's not really much you can do about it. You have to accept it."

The super urgent waiting list he was placed on is the highest priority of the three tiers of patients waiting for a new heart. Typically, only about four or five people are on the list at any one time in the UK.

Dr Paul Callan, a consultant cardiologist at Wythenshawe Hospital's Heart and Lung Centre, worked with Jackson during his diagnosis and recovery.

"Initially, we used to quote an average wait of seven days on the urgent transplant list," he says. "Now it's up to 14 days. Maybe 10% of patients who are put on the list get too poorly and have to be taken off the list."

That increased waiting time is the result of a reduction in the numbers of organ donors in the UK, with a 9% drop recorded in 2026 compared to the same period last year. There are 8,700 people currently waiting for a donor organ, a figure that NHS Blood and Transplant say is an all-time high.

This Organ Donation Week,, external which runs from 21-28 September, the NHS has launched an urgent response plan to address the decline.

Jackson has yet to meet the family of the donor from which he received his new heart. He says he is considering reaching out to them around the two-year anniversary of his surgery.

For him to make a recovery within that time frame, culminating in playing football in a Transplant World Cup, is "remarkable", according to Dr Callan.

England beat six teams on their way to winning last Friday's final in Frankfurt, scoring 36 goals, but for every player at the tournament there is gratitude that they even have the opportunity to play a football match again.

"It is so important to spread that message, have that conversation about organ donation," says England manager Cross, "because our team only exists for that reason.

"I wouldn't have 16 players to manage if we didn't have organ donation. And England wouldn't have just gone and won a World Cup."

title: Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory
description: Cristiano Ronaldo contemplated retirement after the World Cup but wants to reach 1,000 career goals and help a new-look Portugal thrive before hanging up his boots.
fullText:
Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals.

The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain.

However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night.

In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark.

Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did.

"Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think."

The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want.

"I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football."

Ronaldo is a two-time Nations League winner with Portugal, and he said adding a third title was also an aim alongside his personal ambitions.

"Both aims are important," he said.

"One thousand goals, yes, and the national team. Winning the Nations League, the competition starts tomorrow [Thursday], it's a new age."

Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Young talents including Fabio Silva, Renato Veiga, Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves and Francisco Conceicao all feature in Portugal's squad for this international window.

Ronaldo - who joked he will play on for another decade - says helping his country's newest talents was also a pivotal factor in his decision to continue to represent Portugal.

"This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games," he said.

"For me, the most important thing, I know what I am. I know what I do to be here, to have the success that I have.

"I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired... in 10 years!

"I'm happy with myself. It doesn't matter if I play tomorrow, if I rest the next game. For me, the most important thing is that I feel good."

Speaking at a news conference in Lisbon, Portugal boss Jesus described Ronaldo as a "symbol of Portugal and the national team".

It came after the five-time Ballon d'Or winner addressed the criticism he has faced throughout his career - particularly during his time with some of the great clubs of England, Spain and Italy.

"This [Portugal] is possibly where I have felt most cared," Ronaldo said. "From the fans, I also feel the Portuguese like me.

"I do understand that some TV channels like to criticise me, they've tried to kill me with a shotgun, but I can still move away from it.

"Anyway, I am used to it. For over 20 years I have been doing this, but my memories are with people who love me."
