title: Infantino says Fifa can change as he proposes external review
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of the governance of world football's governing body.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.

In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino said the independent process would "recommend potential improvements".

Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened".

This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash.

In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders".

He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!"

His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not."

Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be".

He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together".

Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football.

"We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association. What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided.

"The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead."

Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan.

The 56-year-old Swiss-Italian Fifa leader will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents.

Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.

Having defiantly clung to power for weeks amid an unprecedented rebellion over his presidency, this is a significant change in tone from Infantino - and the first sign that he may feel he has no choice but to compromise if he is to win another re-election in March.

On October 15th, Fifa's Council will meet for the first time since this crisis began, and Infantino will no doubt hope that this relieves some of the pressure he is under.

But even if he is prepared to accept some changes to the way Fifa is run, will that be enough to win over some of those that have turned against him?

As well as wanting him to step down, many of Infantino's critics want an overhaul of Fifa's governance, with curbs on the president's power (such as a maximum of a single term in office), more separation between the president and the Fifa administration, greater emphasis on human rights and sustainability, and the redistribution of Fifa's cash reserves.

It will be fascinating to see if Infantino is prepared to accept such changes if it means staying in power.

title: The Apocalypse Will Not Be Sexy
description: When we picture the end of the world, the first thing that springs to mind is typically the cinematic version of “things going wrong.” We picture the musical score rising to a crescendo…
fullText:
When we picture the end of the world, the first thing that springs to mind is typically the cinematic version of “things going wrong.” We picture the musical score rising to a crescendo as the climactic events take place.  Our heroes are fighting to stop some big giant, unstoppable threat. Even if they are ultimately doomed, there is something noble and exhilarating in going down fighting. And if our heroes somehow survive failure and make it to the post-apocalypse, they usually still have great hair, even though civilization has collapsed.

Put another way, in the movies, the apocalypse is usually pretty sexy.

Of course, in reality disaster is often much more mundane – something closer to dumb and sad than to sexy — as Randall Munroe pointed out years ago in a slightly different context:

A lot of attention is being paid at the moment to an entire culture that has grown up around the “AI Safety” world that is intently focused on stories of doom and the threatened end of humanity. That’s big, attention getting, and splashy. The tabloid version of this culture — the group houses, the polyamory, the recruitment dynamics that a lot of people are suddenly discovering — is even splashier still.

Taken as a whole, this specific version of AI safety is getting a lot of oxygen right now. It’s easy to see why — as a kind of “sexy apocalypse” these narratives, while frightening, are an exciting fantasy, even if they would be an awful reality.  But that heightened fantasy is not what AI safety is actually about.

It’s not about protecting us from the unlikely sexy apocalypse.  It’s about protecting us from the far more likely, and far more numerous, stupid apocalypses along the way.

This mismatch between cinematic safety and actual safety happens all the time. During the Manhattan Project, Edward Teller got some attention by worrying that the Trinity Test might set the entirety of Earth’s atmosphere on fire. Very cinematic! Very concerning! But, as with most things, the reality was much more mundane. Actual experts looked at Teller’s concern, ran the boring calculations, and ruled it out as a threat long before the actual test. That is how safety often works: boring, process-heavy work… that kills off the really sexy scenario.

Instead of global immolation, the real risks came from otherwise smart people doing dumb shit, such as the infamous Demon Core incident, where physicist Louis Slotin exposed himself, and a number of others, to a lethal dose of radiation by trying to use a simple screwdriver head to separate a plutonium core from a reflector… and slipping. Incredibly, this was the second time a mistake like this had happened, with the exact same plutonium core, and Enrico Fermi himself had warned Slotin he’d be dead within a year if he kept it up. Turns out he was right.

For all the talk of “AI Safety” risk these days, the most present real risks remain variations on the theme of “humans doing stupid shit”. Sometimes really smart humans. But stupid actions by humans are a lot less headline grabbing than the shiny sexy apocalypse. A human accidentally causing a radioactive chain reaction by carelessly using a screwdriver to separate things is stupid. Skynet turning everyone into paperclips… is kind of cool and fun.

But, as anyone who works in risk mitigation (including one of the authors of this piece) can tell you, the overwhelming majority of actual disasters aren’t cool and fun. Instead, they’re usually more like the Demon Core: stupid, disappointing, and easily prevented if only a few common sense steps had been taken.

As evidence, one need only to look at the world right now. Most people — perhaps outside of Mike Judge — would not have predicted that the world economy would be on the brink of collapse because the US is run by a group of chud idiots, who think trade is a scam, strategy is woke, and diplomacy is for girls. The current troubles the world is facing are not due to out of control science. They’re due to the American electorate putting aggressively ignorant people into office again.

The most recent flare-up of doom talk traces back to the highly publicized hacking of Hugging Face by an OpenAI model that was being evaluated. As has now been dissected repeatedly, the case involved a model being tested with deliberately lowered guardrails against the ExploitGym benchmark. Told to score as well as possible and not to stop until it had, the model landed on the laziest and most obvious strategy if one has no guardrails: cheat on the test. It then used an unknown exploit in OpenAI’s own sandbox to reach the open internet and quietly broke into Hugging Face looking for those answers.

There was, clearly, a step up in capabilities here. The tool was testing its ability to find exploits and it certainly found some unexpected ones in its pursuit of the ExploitGym benchmark answers. And it’s easy to see how capabilities of this kind could lead to innumerable stupid disasters, like flash crashing the internet through poorly fenced-in systems mindlessly hacking websites to complete some relatively trivial goal.  What happened with that matters in understanding AI safety, but the framing of it as evidence of malicious will on the part of an AI system has sent people off to chase fictional monsters.

The incident wasn’t Terminator-style “rogue AI” doing anything. All of the mistakes that led up to this were, as Eryk Salvaggio points out at the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, fundamentally human mistakes. Employees at OpenAI deliberately disabled the guardrails, they gave the tool an effectively impossible task while telling it not to stop until it had accomplished the task, and they (accidentally!) left a door open for the tool to reach the internet and fan out. These are all human mistakes. Stupid, disappointing, easily preventable. Like using a screwdriver to prop open a plutonium core.

And if we know anything, we know that humans will keep making mistakes like this, and not just because we’re stupid. Slotin wasn’t stupid. The OpenAI researchers who turned off the guardrails weren’t stupid. They were smart people doing dumb things. These sorts of “banal disasters” are the failure mode that we can and should be focused on minimizing because, while they can be just as damaging as the grand and cinematic versions, they are (self-evidently) far more likely to happen, because they only require stupid decisions to accomplish. No brilliant breakthroughs or novel technologies are required — just people doing stupid things because they’re overconfident in their own abilities — or overconfident because the talking machine confidently told them to be.

Unfortunately, doing the real safety work in the tech world to prevent these kinds of human disasters is often some combination of boring, depressing, and unpopular. Yes, you have to think like adversaries and consider what actions they might take, but those adversaries tend not to be god-like beings looking to turn us into paperclips. They tend to be things like teenagers trying to get around the restrictions their parents have put on their devices. Or people trying to spam systems for commercial intent.

This essential nuts-and-bolts safety work also doesn’t, typically, require brilliant and manly heroes to nobly die for the ashes of their fathers and the temples of their gods.  Instead, the hard work of actual safety requires things that are much less sexy: empathy, conflicting values, and a deep understanding of tradeoffs that will never fully resolve. Those qualities are not highly esteemed in the present moment. But they are critical for tackling the actual threats and the actual risks, which aren’t as flashy, and don’t make for such fun headlines. AI safety matters, but we’re unlikely to move in the direction of actual safety if all the focus is on fantastical stories involving killer robots.

But that’s not what the media wants to talk about these days — and, tragically, it also doesn’t seem to be what the CEOs of the frontier labs are all that interested in these days either. There are real AI safety issues we should be taking seriously, and none of them have to do with whether some frontier model decides it wants to play a game of thermonuclear war.

Dave Willner is the co-founder of Zentropi, formerly the head of trust & safety at OpenAI, of community policy at Airbnb, and of content policy at Facebook.

Mike Masnick is the founder, editor, and CEO of Techdirt and has been staring into the abyss of internet safety questions for far too long.

fullText:
Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper

Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models.

It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips, and other critical components, for electronics, including phones.

The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers.

“Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.”

Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, Apple is pricing them as current products, he adds.

The iPhone is not the first product to have a “RAMageddon” price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.

Other manufacturers of smartphones have also increased the price of new models, with Samsung and Google adding up to £80 to their flagship phones.

Apple has also increased the price of its refurbished stock by £60 to £70, including the older iPhone 15 that is no longer sold new in the shops. However, according to data from Uswitch, the increase in cost has yet to reach the third-party refurbished iPhone market.

“A refurbished iPhone 16 has held at about £503 all summer, roughly where it was before the 18 Pro launch,” says Ernest Doku, a Uswitch mobiles expert. “A refurbished 14 is about £10 cheaper than it was in June, while the 16 has simply stopped falling in price.”

Most smartphone makers, other than Apple, have discontinued older models that were no longer economically viable, and likely wouldn’t sell at higher prices. The impact has been particularly acute at the lower end of the market.

In its latest forecast, IDC predicts there will be the steepest annual contraction in worldwide smartphone sales on record this year, falling almost 17% to just over 1bn handsets. “People are buying fewer phones and paying considerably more for those they do buy,” Jeronimo says.

There have been bigger price rises for other electronics. Computer makers, which are much more exposed to rapidly jumping memory and chip costs, have had to raise prices several times over the past 18 months.

Microsoft added up to £220 to some of its Surface computers but also released versions with half as much memory as a way to attempt to keep prices down.

The move has forced the company to try to redesign Windows to run more comfortably with only 8GB of RAM, which it hasn’t for several years.

Many of PC maker Dell’s high-end laptops have jumped by as much as 25%, while the repairable laptop maker Framework has had to continually adjust prices as costs fluctuate.

Even Apple added £100 to its lower-cost MacBook Neo, as well as rises to most models in its Mac and iPad lines in June. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” the company says in a statement.

Games consoles aren’t immune, either. In a rare state of affairs, Microsoft recently increased the price of its near six-year-old console to £670, up from its original launch price of £449.

“Console storage and memory prices have increased by more than 2.5 times, and we expect another doubling by the autumn of 2027,” the company says.

Unfortunately, £100 added to the cost of a phone may only be the start of the price pain, with key memory producers, including SK Hynix, suggesting the shortages could last beyond 2030.

Jeronimo says memory prices are going to continue rising well into 2027, even if the pace has slowed from the “extraordinary spikes” seen earlier this year. “Even once memory costs ease, I do not expect smartphone prices to fall back to the same levels as last year.

“Increases in this industry tend to be sticky. Once customers have absorbed a higher price and manufacturers have rebuilt their margins, companies hold the line and add value through storage or features, rather than cutting the ticket price.”

The bad news for consumers is that “the era of cheap smartphones – or any device to be honest – is over,” Jeronimo says.

title: Bred for success - why Backstedt can hit cycling's peaks
description: Zoe Backstedt won world time trial silver in Montreal aged just 21 and the multiple junior world champion plans to win much more.
fullText:
The beaming smile fits the remarkable achievement. The words offer up the tinge of regret from a potential cycling great in the making.

"I have to say I'm happy, but at the same time of course I also came here for a gold medal," said Zoe Backstedt, shortly after collecting time trial silver at cycling's Road World Championships in Montreal.

The response also demonstrates both a youthful exuberance and a maturity not all can muster, even well beyond Backstedt's 21 years.

"To be still 21, my first elite and still eligible for the under-23s, to be second is really incredible and I've had a smile on my face since the second I crossed the line. It's been a really cool day," she added.

But then the Welsh talent - who will celebrate her 22nd birthday later this week - has already been winning for years, having been raised from a successful cycling family and, many have long agreed, destined for the very top of the sport.

GB's Backstedt wins world time-trial silver

Women's cycling could be unstoppable - Backstedt

Welsh teenager follows lead of Olympic great Kenny

Backstedt carries a famous name around with her.

Her father Magnus won the famous cobbled Paris-Roubaix one-day race and a stage of the Tour de France during a lengthy career as a professional, before moving into coaching and broadcasting.

Her mother Megan won the British Road Race national title, competed for Great Britain at World Championships and for Wales at the Commonwealth Games.

Her older sister Elynor is also a talented professional cyclist with back-to-back medals at the Junior Road World Championships in 2018 and 2019.

"For a long, long time I actually hated cycling," Zoe, the youngest of the family, once told the BBC.

"It took me until I was maybe 10 or 11 to enjoy it.

"At the time I was doing cycling, netball, tennis and athletics all at once. I'd go out on the bike, but I'd say to dad that I don't want to do any more than two hours. I was adamant.

"Then one day it just clicked and I thought this is what I want to do."

At 17, Backstedt became the youngest ever winner of a women's elite cycling race in Belgium, with a cyclo-cross win in Essen.

Having claimed the Junior World Road Race gold in Flanders in 2021, a year down the line she not only retained her title but also added the time-trial crown.

In 2025, still only 20 and riding her first world under-23 time trial, she demolished the field, finishing one minute 51 seconds ahead of her nearest rival on a hilly course in Rwanda.

Again, her post-race words gave a deep insight into her sporting determination.

"It's brutal climbing here, but I really like it," she said after conquering a course which included a punishing cobbled incline.

It has not all been plain sailing. In 2024, sickness meant she missed out on a chance to ride at the Paris Olympics.

Her 2025 cyclo-cross season was interrupted by a broken hand and wrist, which kept her out of racing until January of this year, when she returned with seventh in the women's elite race at the Cyclo-Cross World Championships in Hulst, Netherlands.

When you are as determined - and talented - as Zoe Backstedt, such setbacks can be merely launching pads for even better to come.

Back on the road in June, she took her ninth professional victory - winning a sprint stage at the Tour de Suisse Femmes.

Over the next 10 days she doubled up at the British Road Championships - first successfully defending her elite time-trial crown before winning her first British road race title with another emphatic victory in Aberystwyth.

In July, she retained the Baloise Ladies Tour title, a year after becoming the youngest winner of the race.

She rode the Tour de France Femmes for the first time in August - a "goosebumps" moment, she told the BBC - finishing a creditable fourth in the time-trial stage.

And now, in September - having declined the opportunity to defend her U23 title - she finished second to 35-year-old Swiss Marlen Reusser who retained her elite world time trial crown in Canada.

"I'm over the moon with my performance," Backstedt told the BBC after a few hours to reflect on her ride.

"It was really a crazy long time trial so to take home the silver medal, I'm super proud of that."

Backstedt is not finished yet either in Montreal. On Saturday, 26 September she will line up as one of the leaders for Great Britain in the road race.

"It's going to be a hard course, that's for sure," said Backstedt.

"But myself and Lauren Dixon will be the leaders and I think with the team that we've got coming, we will make it a really hard race."

A hard race, just the way she likes it.

She has no intention of making life easier by concentrating on one cycling discipline.

"I would like to continue across them all," Backstedt said.

"I think it's something I really enjoy.

"Time-trialling, road, cyclocross, they're all three disciplines that I really love doing and I love racing so I can't really say if I would choose one or the other.

"I think putting all of them in there and doing a lot of work for all of them is what makes me stronger by the end of the season as well, so I will continue to race all of them."

And, almost certainly, Backstedt will continue to win more medals too.

title: Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad

fullText:
Rob Hawkins is among five Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup winners who will attempt to help England defend the trophy in Australia this autumn.

Hawkins, Wheelchair Super League's top try-scorer this season with 70, scored four tries as Halifax Panthers completed a domestic treble by beating Leeds Rhinos to win Sunday's Grand Final.

He is joined in England's 10-player final World Cup squad by club-mates Jack Brown - who scored six tries in that final - and Finlay O'Neill.

Both Hawkins and Brown were part of the England squad who defeated France dramatically at Manchester Central in November 2022 to win the World Cup.

So too was Lewis King, who will captain England down under, plus King's London Roosters club-mate Joe Coyd and Leeds Rhinos' Nathan Collins.

Collins will be joined in the England squad by Leeds team-mate Tristan Norfolk, Roosters' Mason Billington and the Sheffield Eagles pair of Luis Domingos and Chris Haynes.

England face Wales on Friday, 30 October (04:30 GMT) in their opening match at the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup - which will be staged alongside the men's and women's tournaments.

They then face the USA on Tuesday, 3 November (07:30 GMT) and Ireland on Friday, 6 November (06:00 GMT), aiming to secure a spot in the following Tuesday's semi-finals.

The wheelchair tournament will be staged at the Wollongong Entertainment Centre, with the final on Friday, 13 November (08:30 GMT).

England head coach Tom Coyd - who led the side to their World Cup success in Manchester four years ago - said: "Every player understands what it means to wear the England shirt and the responsibility that comes with it.

"Yesterday's brilliant Wheelchair Super League Grand Final was a testament to the special community that we are privileged to represent on the world stage."

England's wheelchair squad will fly out to Australia on 22 October.

England squad: Mason Billington (London Roosters), Jack Brown (Halifax Panthers), Nathan Collins (Leeds Rhinos), Joe Coyd (London Roosters), Luis Domingos (Sheffield Eagles), Rob Hawkins (Halifax Panthers), Chris Haynes (Sheffield Eagles), Lewis King (London Roosters), Tristan Norfolk (Leeds Rhinos), Finlay O'Neill (Halifax Panthers).

title: Wales will have no fear in Portugal - James
description: Jordan James insists depleted Wales will not be overawed against "the best players in the world" in their Nations League A opener against Portugal on Thursday.
fullText:
Jordan James insists depleted Wales will not be overawed when they line up against "the best players in the world" in their Nations League A opener against Portugal on Thursday.

A Wales squad already missing the likes of Joe Rodon and Dylan Lawlor has been hit by the withdrawals of Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead and star man Harry Wilson.

Having returned to the top tier of the Nations League by winning their League B group in 2024, Wales begin what looks like being a demanding campaign as they meet a star-studded Portuguese side in Lisbon.

Portugal can call on a string of star names including Ruben Dias, Joao Cancelo, Nuno Mendes, Vitinha, Joao Neves and Bruno Fernandes, not to mention 41-year-old Cristiano Ronaldo.

But Wolverhampton Wanderers midfielder James says Wales will have "no fear" as they go in search of a first win since last November's World Cup qualifying triumph against North Macedonia.

"Obviously they're the best players in the world at the end of the day, you can't really sugarcoat it," James said.

Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"They've got Champions League winners, they've got these kinds of things.

"I think we're always underdogs. We're used to it, so hopefully we can use that to benefit ourselves.

"You can't count us out. We've got a puncher's chance at the end of the day and we're going there to sort of cause an upset."

James is likely to be in direct competition with a Portuguese midfield regarded by some as the best in world football.

In Portugal's most recent game, the 1-0 defeat by Spain in the round of 16 at this summer's World Cup, Paris St-Germain duo Neves and Vitinha lined up at the base of midfield with Manchester United captain Fernandes in front of them.

But 21-cap James has faced similar challenges before in his young career, having memorably produced a stellar performance when Wales beat a Croatia team featuring a midfield three of Luka Modric, Marcelo Brozovic and Mateo Kovacic in October 2023.

"I've still got Kovacic's shirt on the game up in my room," said James, who was 19 at the time of the Croatia triumph.

"That was a really proud moment for me at such a young age to be able to compete against the best.

"It was a really proud moment and hopefully there will be many, many more."

James says he does not get nervous about facing star names – although he did feel "a bit star-struck" when he lined up for Leicester City against Frank Lampard's Coventry City last season because the former England midfielder is his idol.

James, who was born 11 months after Ronaldo joined Manchester United the first time in 2003, describes the prospect of facing the former Real Madrid forward as "a bit mad".

He says Ronaldo's career – which has so far included 146 international goals over 23 years – is a result of superhuman qualities.

"We're all trying to achieve the same thing, to be the best player in the world," James said.

"But you get those sort of aliens in a way that don't seem human. You look at the Messis, the Neymars, the Ronaldos - they've just got that extra little quality where in big moments they turn up and can do it again and again and again.

"I think that's the main thing. The longevity of how they're able to do it is unbelievable."

title: Carse needs time away, says 'good mate' Brook
description: England white-ball captain Harry Brook says his "very good mate" Brydon Carse needs time away from international cricket.
fullText:
England white-ball captain Harry Brook said his "very good mate" Brydon Carse needs time away from international cricket.

Pace bowler Carse was arrested then de-arrested on a night out in Derby in August.

On Friday, Derbyshire Police confirmed an investigation into an alleged assault has ended, with no further action taken.

Carse now faces an investigation by the Cricket Regulator.

Though he remains available for England selection, he has not been chosen in any format of the game since the incident.

Batter Brook is a close friend of the Durham seamer and the pair share an agent.

"I'm very good mates with Carsey," Brook told BBC Sport.

"I've spoken a lot with him. I think he just needs time away from the international scene.

"He's working on a few things behind the scenes and hopefully he'll be ready at some point in the future."

Brook has endured his own tough period off the field – in October last year he was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington on the eve of a one-day international against New Zealand.

The 27-year-old said he would be able to pass on his experience of dealing with controversy.

Though Carse, 31, is available for England selection, the England and Wales Cricket Board has said he will "take time" to "work through the issues that led to the Derby incident".

White-ball head coach Brendon McCullum said Carse needs to "get his house order" before he can play for England again.

At the weekend, new Test coach Stephen Fleming discussed the "standards" England players must meet.

Before Tuesday's first one-day international against Sri Lanka at Chester-le-Street, Brook said there will eventually be a "debate" over the prospects of Carse receiving a recall.

"He's a very good cricketer, we all know that," said Brook.

"He's been bowling extremely well for Durham. When his time for selection is up, that will be a debate."

Leg-spinner Adil Rashid will miss the opener to the three-match series against Sri Lanka because of a hand injury.

With Jacob Bethell already absent following knee surgery, Tom Banton will open the batting.

England hammered the tourists 3-0 in a one-sided T20 series last week. Brook's team have been superb in the shortest format, winning 23 of their past 26 completed internationals.

But the next global tournament is the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa in October and November 2027, and Brook said that 50-over cricket will now be given priority.

"Naturally it does, with the World Cup being next year," said Brook.

"That's not saying we're taking anything away from T20 cricket at all, because we're absolutely flying in that format at the minute.

"With the World Cup being just around the corner, and now we've solidified qualification, we can really start to home in on what the squad and XI is."

Tuesday's game in Durham will be England's first ODI since adding Kevin Pietersen to their backroom staff.

Former England batter Pietersen has been recruited as a mentor for the build-up to the 50-over World Cup. On Monday, he began the hosts' training with a session on how to play spin bowling.

Brook's side are now on a diet of white-ball cricket up to the Test tour of South Africa in December.

Before then, and following the conclusion of the series against Sri Lanka on Sunday, they travel to Pakistan in October for a one-day tri-series that also includes the Sri Lankans.

In November, England are in Australia for three ODIs and five T20s against their Ashes rivals.

The T20 series in Australia finishes a week before England's sole warm-up game in South Africa.

Because of the tight turnaround, some of the multi-format fast bowlers are likely to be rested for the T20s in Australia, meaning a break for the likes of Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue, Gus Atkinson and possibly Sonny Baker.

The squads for the tours of Pakistan and Australia are set to be named next week, along with a new batch of central contracts. The group to tour South Africa for Fleming's first series in charge will come in October.

Meanwhile, Jonathan Trott has been named England Lions head coach for their winter tours of West Indies, South Africa and Sri Lanka.

Former England batter Trott's four-year spell in charge of Afghanistan came to an end in February.

A contender for the England Test job before Fleming was appointed in July, Trott replaces Andrew Flintoff, who stepped down in August.

title: How will clubs train during three-week international break?
description: BBC Sport looks at how clubs are planning to deal with the extended three-week international break.
fullText:
The first international break of the season is under way - and this one is longer than fans will have become accustomed to.

For the first time, the Premier League and the Championship will come to a halt for three weeks rather than the usual two.

Football fans tend not to love international breaks, but this change has been done with good intentions.

It merges the four games played in the old September and October breaks into one slot.

So the domestic game stops for three weeks, rather than four weeks across two windows. Club football is actually getting a week back.

But for players not on international duty, three weeks is a long time for finely tuned athletes not to play competitively.

So how are clubs going to deal with this change?

Here's how different teams plan to balance the international break.

Most squads in the Premier League these days are packed with international players, and Brentford are no different.

Most of the Bees' squad are away, with about 12 players - including Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago - left at their training facility, including five who are coming back from injury.

Brentford have a longer break than almost every other team, given they hosted Chelsea on Friday evening.

Boss Keith Andrews has given his first-team players a week off with individual training programmes to follow. Those players will not have restrictions on leaving the country, but it is unlikely long-haul flights would be sanctioned.

The squad will reconvene on Saturday, 26 September to begin training again, before playing a behind-closed-doors game against another English club on the weekend of 3 October.

That friendly could potentially give the likes of Nathan Collins and Sepp van den Berg a chance to return to action, with the rest of the squad made up of under-21 players.

The second international break will look very different, with the Bees playing Brighton on Sunday, 8 November and back in action against Everton on Saturday, 21 November.

Players may be given the odd day off, but in general it will be a normal training programme with no friendly before the usual preparation for the fixture against the Toffees.

Liverpool, meanwhile, will carry on training with the small number of players that remain, with a few days off.

Manager Andoni Iraola says he will be left with "no more than three days probably to prepare" for the home game with Manchester City on 11 October.

Aston Villa have a very different international break planned.

Unai Emery will return to former club Sevilla, where he won the Europa League three times on the bounce.

Sevilla and Villa will face off in the 15th edition of the Antonio Puerta Trophy on Friday, 2 October.

The game is played in memory of the 22-year-old Sevilla wing-back, who died on 28 August 2007 after having multiple cardiac arrests on the pitch during a La Liga game against Getafe.

While Premier League teams see their squads decimated by international call-ups, it is not quite as dramatic in the Championship.

Many clubs will only have a handful, such as Blackburn Rovers with just four call-ups.

For Rovers boss Tony Mowbray this break will be a positive for a couple of reasons.

Mowbray has had to contend with an injury crisis in the early part of the season, with more than 10 players ruled out in the opening weeks.

The break gives Rovers the chance to ease some of those players back into action, such as Gady Beyuku and Moussa Baradji who recently made their comebacks, and others close to a return like Scott Wharton.

After the trip to Portsmouth on Saturday, Rovers headed back to Lancashire and will have a few days on the training ground this week.

After such a busy start to the campaign, with league fixtures and the Carabao Cup, it also gives Mowbray - who returned to the club in the summer - a chance to properly work with his players.

But it will not all be training.

Mowbray intends to give the players a few days off from the end of the week. Players such as Yuri Ribeiro will be able to return home to Portugal, if they so wish.

The cycle will then be repeated the following week, training the first half with a short break over the weekend. Then for week three, it is back to the usual pre-match routine before the home game against Cardiff.

Mowbray is also looking to find a Premier League or League One team to play in a behind-closed-doors friendly.

It will help those returning from injury to get minutes in the bank, and keep other members of the squad ticking over.

In the two-week break in November, players may still get a short spell off while matches are more likely to be in-house affairs with teams made up of senior and under-21 players.

The three-week international break might have posed a unique situation for a couple of clubs, whereby they could have a full squad and no games to play.

League One carries on playing unless clubs get three call-ups which meet the EFL's criteria, then a postponement can be requested.

Only four of the 12 matches have survived on each of the two weekends.

Yet many clubs prepared in advance by scheduling Football League Trophy fixtures during these three weeks.

Clubs tend to rotate in this competition anyway, so the games still go ahead even if league games are postponed.

Twelve teams will play two trophy ties, with 10 clubs playing once.

That left just Leyton Orient and Reading at risk at not having a game to play. Both have only had one league match called off, so will not have all three weeks vacant.

title: Elon Musk's spending draws additional attention to Texas Senate race
description:
Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in the Senate race in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images file)
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.
In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.
Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.
fullText:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”

The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.

So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

title: Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump reportedly calls off airstrikes
description:
, Timour Azhari and Jana Choukeir
RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.

fullText:
RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.

A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group ‌this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed ‌bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.

The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes on Sunday against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the ​last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.

Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, asked Trump by phone on Sunday for US military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the sources, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of support during the call.

Riyadh was apparently struck on Saturday for the first time since the escalation began, with explosions heard and smoke visible near the airport. The Houthis said they had fired missiles at the Saudi capital; the Saudis ‌have not commented.

The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since ⁠2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.

Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.

According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. Nearly 130,000 ⁠Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.

Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.

Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at ​the ​Red Sea's mouth and the government's base in Aden, the sources said.

"The government forces appear to remain largely in a ​defensive posture following the loss of the Bab el-Mandeb area, while the Houthis are ‌seeking to maintain the momentum of their advance, despite being exposed to intensive air strikes," said Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist now working as a political analyst.

"These mountains could become critical to determining whether the Houthis succeed in consolidating their recent territorial gains or whether government forces will be able to retain the positions necessary to mount a counteroffensive."

The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched as "Operation Epic Fury" in February against Iran.

The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire, and has kept out of the Yemen conflict since.

The Houthis' Red Sea advance risks cutting off the main alternative route Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports ‌that bypass disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of ​tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the ​cargo's value to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in ​the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.

Traders say Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of oil both this month and next, to be loaded from ‌off Oman on the far side of Hormuz. Satellite data shows Saudi exports through ​Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, ​up from just 700,000 in August.

That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industries are still paying record prices for some refined fuels, with the US retail price of diesel hitting another all-time high on Monday.

In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship ​sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries ‌to crew. It also said it had learned of an earlier strike on a gas tanker.

Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the ​United States and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Tuesday to New York to attend the UN General Assembly.

title: Celtic struggling to be 'on same script' - Carter-Vickers

But Carter-Vickers told Sky Sports: "I agree with the manager - I don't think there was much in the game. Neither team were particularly good. There's a lot we can improve on, but I'm confident in the group we have."

Asked why Celtic's season had taken a downturn with two losses to their city rivals either side of Europa League defeat by Ferencvaros, the United States international added: "Hard to put your finger on one thing.

"We played a bit too random. We need to get better at that, getting a script and sticking to it.

"The last two games we've played have been big pressure games. As players, you rely on having something to fall back on.

"We haven't had the time to get that. As players, we can do better for sure. It's something we can improve on.

"There's a lot of new players at the club. It's about getting everyone on the same script. The group are together like we've always been. We need to find consistency."

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk insists he is "focusing on the "present" and there is "nothing to report" when it comes to his Anfield contract.

The 35-year-old's deal expires at the end of this season and it remains to be seen whether the centre-back, who joined Liverpool from Southampton in January 2018, will be offered an extension or he will choose to move on.

Van Dijk has played every minute of Liverpool's Premier League campaign so farand said his side have "not had a bad start" under new boss Andoni Iraola.

"We've not had a bad start - we could have done better in a couple of games, but we are where we are. On to the next."

Van Dijk will now head off on international duty after holding positive talks about his Netherlands future with new manager Xavi, who was at Anfield to watch Liverpool's Champions League opener against Atletico Madrid earlier this month.

Barcelona will be heading into the international break with the best start to a season in quite time now, with the team having won all their matches in all competitions.

However, the ecstasy of that success was slightly muted after Andreas Christensen's injury against Sevilla.

The Dane could be out for up to six weeks by rough estimates, leaving Barcelona without a key defensive options as we enter a tricky part of the campaign.

Given Christensen's injury, it is only natural to expect Barcelona to step up their efforts when it comes to eyeing defensive reinforcements.

According to UmDois Deportes (h/t SPORT), the club have already kickstarted their preparations, as they are keeping close tabs on Arthur Dias.

Dias dueling with former Barcelona star Memphis Depay. (Photo by Heuler Andrey/Getty Images)

A left-footed centre-back by trade, Dias currently plies hits trade for Athletico PR and has been recently called up by Carlo Ancelotti to the Brazilian national team.

The report suggests Barcelona scout Joao Amaral was in Curitiba this weekend to witness Dias in action against Bahia.

Barcelona, though, could face stiff competition for Dias, with Tottenham Hotspur along with Como, Newcastle United and Benfica also interested in his services. Athletico PR had already rejected a bid from Tottenham in the summer.

It is clear that Barcelona are in the running to sign Arthur Dias despite increasing competition. And given the player's profile, it is easy to wonder why.

Does Dias have what it takes to thrive at Barcelona? (Photo by Heuler Andrey/Getty Images)

Aged just 19, Dias is an ambidextrous centre-back, who has shown a high level of physicality and maturity for his age. He already has 50 competitive appearances to his name for Athletico PR.

Other than his physicality and a 1.88m frame, the young Brazilian is also known for his ball-playing ability. He is adept at both short passes or passes in between the line, making him a natural fit for Barcelona's style of play.

title: League B return, no Bradley and Kvaratskhelia test - NI talking points
description: Northern Ireland's return to Uefa Nations League B will see them face a player manager Michael O'Neill calls "one of the best in the world" but they enter the campaign without their own captain.
fullText:
The build-up to Northern Ireland's 2026 Nations League campaign has been dominated by the future of Ceadach O'Neill and the always thorny issue of eligibility.

With the Arsenal forward included in Michael O'Neill's 28-man squad for this four-game window, the 18-year-old appears set to add to his two senior caps across the next two weeks, likely ruling out any future switch of international allegiance despite an approach from the Republic of Ireland.

While one prominent storyline seems as if it will soon be put to bed, there is plenty more to look out for as Northern Ireland make their return to League B.

NI squad only picked on merit - O'Neill

O'Neill and Graham retain places in NI squad

For the first time since June 2022, Northern Ireland will face four games in the same international window.

Starting away to Georgia on 25 September and finishing at home to the same opposition on 5 October, in between Michael O'Neill's side will face Hungary at Windsor Park and Ukraine in Slovakia.

The manager has named a 28-man panel for the games, compared to bringing 23 players along for June's double-header of friendlies against Guinea and France.

O'Neill said the schedule was challenging but that his team "must deal" with the change given the four-game window will be used again this time next year in Euro 2028 qualifying.

"I think for a smaller association, it poses more challenges if I'm honest. If a player picks up a calf strain the Saturday before we meet up, he's going to miss four games. It's a window that, I believe, is more beneficial for the bigger nations.

"I'm sure within the period, players will get injured, two bookings and I think you're suspended as well. It will be challenging, but it's the way the window will be going forward."

The campaign represents a step up in quality as well as quantity, not least when facing a player O'Neill calls one of the best in the world in Georgia's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia,

While Northern Ireland have sought friendlies against Spain, France, Sweden and Denmark across the past two and a half years, as well as facing Germany in World Cup qualifying, these will be the side's first games in the second tier of the Nations League since 2020.

Topping a League C group also containing Luxembourg, Belarus and Bulgaria last time around was enough to ensure a backdoor route into the World Cup play-offs this year where Northern Ireland were beaten 2-0 by Italy in Bergamo.

Naturally, promotion ensures securing such a safety net for Euro 2028 will be tougher, but League B status does mean a top-two finish in the group would see them in the second band of seeds for December's qualifying draw.

"I do think it's a group that is quite well matched in terms of where the teams are," said O'Neill.

"Obviously some of the teams are ranked a lot higher than us, I don't think we should be frightened by that.

"I think the games will be extremely tough, but I think it's a great challenge."

Reflecting on his role with Fifa's Technical Study Group at the World Cup, O'Neill said it was noteworthy to see how many games "were decided by individual brilliance" rather that general superiority of winning teams.

Once again, however, the manager will have to do without the player in his own squad most likely to produce such moments.

While Isaac Price has been a more regular source of goals, Liverpool's Conor Bradley has a talismanic quality. Since the beginning of 2025, however, the 23-year-old has endured a luckless run to miss seven Northern Ireland's games through either injury or suspension.

Still on the sidelines after January knee surgery, Bradley is expected to be absent for the entirety of this campaign, with O'Neill telling BBC Sport NI last month that it would be a "bonus" to see his captain before the start of Euro 2028 qualifying in March.

Since a 1-0 win over Scotland in March 2024, the occasion of Bradley's first international goal, Northern Ireland have averaged 1.5 goals a game in 16 internationals with him in the side compared to just 0.7 goals per game in the seven he has missed.

Finding a different creative spark in Bradley's absence will be key to the campaign.

While there was naturally disappointment after that loss to Italy in March, there has long been a sense that this group's best chance of major tournament qualification lies in the years ahead.

Of the starting XI that featured in Bergamo, only Hull City's 31-year-old defender Paddy McNair is older than 26.

The average age of the 28-man squad named last week was just 24-years-old with a quartet of teenagers - Ceadach O'Neill, Kieran Morrison, Braiden Graham and Tom Atcheson - giving the panel an even more youthful look.

In addition to McNair, the only two other players in the squad older than 30 are central striking options Dion Charles, 30, and Josh Magennis, 36.

O'Neill, however, is expected to stick with the 21-year-old Jamie Donley up top as he continues to build for the qualification campaigns ahead.

The Tottenham Hotspur player has scored twice in 10 caps and started the past five games for Northern Ireland, but he endured a difficult 2025-26 season at club level on loan at Stoke City and Oxford United.

Despite featuring for Spurs during pre-season, he will spend this year with Luton Town, back on loan in League One where he impressed for Leyton Orient in 2024-25.

"What happened with Jamie last year was not really of Jamie's doing," said O'Neill.

"The game time at Stoke was, I think, unfair on the player, to be honest. The second loan he gets injured in his first game but the games he did play, he did well.

"I think the thing for Jamie is just to play regularly. I think he's got all the attributes of a top, young player. He's still a Tottenham player on a long-term contract and I think he's gone to a good club (in Luton)."

title: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
description: Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday...
fullText:
Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’

The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”.

“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”

Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models.

US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down.

However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy”, adding that a slowdown could give China the edge.

On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”.

Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account.

Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems.

“You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.”

He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.”

On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations.

However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so.

“The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper. “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern.

“Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”

fullText:
As world leaders prepare to gather in New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this week, a growing number of flashpoints across the Middle East are raising concerns about a wider regional escalation, from renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen to fresh warnings exchanged between Washington and Tehran.

A dramatic Houthi offensive in Yemen has emerged as one of the most significant developments heading into UNGA.

The Iran-backed group has seized key territory in recent weeks, including a strategically important island in the Red Sea and coastal areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a crucial maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. US and Gulf officials have expressed growing concern that the Houthis are seeking to establish greater control over the waterway, which is vital to global trade and energy shipments.

Despite receiving increased US intelligence and targeting support, Saudi Arabia has struggled to halt the Houthi advance. CNN reported Friday that Gulf and American officials are increasingly doubtful Riyadh can reverse the Houthi gains on its own.

The fighting has intensified sharply in recent days. Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, while the Houthis claimed they shot down a Saudi F‑15 fighter jet over Yemen. On Saturday, the group also claimed missile and drone attacks on “sensitive” sites in Riyadh and an Aramco oil facility in Yanbu.

The latest exchanges underscore fears that Yemen is becoming an increasingly important front in the broader regional confrontation involving Iran.

Amid the worsening security environment, the US State Department and several US diplomatic missions have urged Americans in the region to exercise increased caution.

On Saturday, the State Department warned that the conflict “has the potential to escalate rapidly” and advised heightened vigilance.

Separately, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a security alert restricting travel by US government personnel to the cities of Taif and Yanbu without special authorization.

The warnings come as officials monitor the possibility of additional attacks involving Iran, Iranian-aligned groups and US partners in the region.

Iran’s central military command said Sunday it had received information suggesting the United States, with support from regional partners, could be preparing new military action against Iran.

In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim News Agency, Iran warned that any new US attack would trigger sustained strikes on US bases and interests across the region. Tehran also warned that countries assisting such operations would be considered parties to the conflict.

There have been no publicly reported US strikes on Iran for more than two weeks.

US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, further raised tensions with remarks indicating major decisions on Iran may be approaching.

Speaking to Fox News, Trump said he was in “deciding mode” and that “very big things” could happen soon. According to Fox correspondent Trey Yingst, Trump outlined three possible outcomes for Iran: a deal with Washington, increased economic pressure or military action.

At the same time, Trump said his administration remains in contact with the Houthis and is still avoiding direct US military involvement in the group’s conflict with Saudi Arabia.

Regional diplomacy is expected to be dominated by discussions on Iran, Yemen, maritime security and energy markets.

Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is leading a delegation, while Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain are all sending senior representatives.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected to attend the General Assembly after the Trump administration approved travel for a core Iranian delegation.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” a State Department spokesperson said Thursday.

With fighting intensifying in Yemen, threats escalating between Washington and Tehran, and energy markets remaining sensitive to disruptions, many diplomats arriving in New York see this year’s General Assembly as taking place under one of the most volatile Middle East security environments in recent years.

CNN’s Tim Lister contributed to this story.

title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It
description: Large language models sometimes behave in ways resembling human emotional responses, and recent work has identified internal representations that may explain this. We ask whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from fear, sadness, and generic negative valence, and whether this representation functions as pain would be expected to. We build a dataset describing painful situations across five categories: physical, psychological, social, moral, and cognitive. These are paired with controls for fear, negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensation, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. Using denoised difference-in-means, we extract a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight models across five families, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters.

title: Croatia Forward Boris Tisma No Longer Part of Washington Basketball
description: One of the Washington Huskies' incoming international signings is no longer set to play for Danny Sprinkle.
fullText:
Despite appearing in practice footage over the past couple of months, incoming Croatian forward Boris Tisma is no longer set to play for the Washington Huskies in the 2026-27 season.

Tisma, one of several reported international signings for UW coach Danny Sprinkle this offseason, has now signed a two-year contract with Movistar Estudiantes, a professional team based in Madrid, Spain. He previously played for Real Madrid in 2020-21 and was then loaned out to another Liga ACB team in 2021.

Prior to the 6-foot-9 power forward's move to America, he played for two teams in Croatia—Split (2022-25) and Zadar (2025-26)—and one SC Derby in Montenegro, proving to be a rising international prospect that attracted the attention of several schools, including UW.

In the past two months, the Huskies have added a pair of transfers, former Rutgers guard Harun Zrno and ex-Nevada guard Tayshawn Comer, but still have a void to fill in the post with the loss of Tisma.
